en: Mirror, Reference Number, Folio Number, Script: Add. Māgadhī (of the Pāla period). *Guhyāvalī* with Commentary. Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Vajrayoginī!
Copper does not turn into gold merely through the great afflictions (*kleśa*) of living beings; likewise, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is not realized even by serving the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, those who possess bodies formed from a mass of merit, who are [otherwise] limited, yet at times have minds as waveless as the ocean of the mudrā—homage to those accomplished ones (*siddha*). (1)
Oṃ, homage to Vajrasattva!
To the Protector who consists of the manifold forms, who is free from conceptualization regarding all mental constructions,
who is liberated from the intrinsic nature of all things, and who accomplishes the welfare of the entire universe.
Having prostrated before that one of great wisdom in the lineage of Daḍīpāda, I,
the monk Śrīghanadeva, shall clearly compose this commentary.

May this handful of flowers be offered by me at the feet of the venerable Vajravilāsinī—those feet which are friends to the purity of realizing non-duality; which illuminate wisdom and compassion; which crush the obstacles for people who are vessels of the sixteen fears; and which shine forth the excellence of the manifestation of the cosmic form revealed to the entire universe.

The glorious Ārya Daupāda, whose heart was permeated with great compassion, having personally realized the samādhi of the unerring, true method through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*), began to compose that very *svādhiṣṭhānakrama* in twenty-five verses for the benefit of all people.
Now, its illumination (*saṃdyota*) sets forth the designation, the designated, the relationship, the purpose, and the ultimate purpose.
Among these, the "designation" is the composition of the teaching.
The subject matter (*abhidheya*) is characterized by unobscured great bliss (*anāvaraṇa-mahāsukha*).
The purpose (*prayojana*) is the direct realization of the path of the union (*yuganaddha*) of unobscured great bliss.
As for the ultimate purpose (*prayojana-prayojana*), it is indeed the fruit of unobscured great bliss called "union," because of the statement: "The path is union; the fruit is union."

Even in the absence of a primary word explicitly indicating the relationship, the relationship characterized as that between the signifier and the signified (*vācaka-vācya*) should be understood through contextual implication (*sāmarthya*).

In this regard, first of all, for those who do not know the oral tradition (*sampradāya*), there is no arising of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) even when there is attachment to external wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, demonstrating the arising of the Great Seal even for those who know the oral tradition when they have attachment to external wisdom, he says: "Copper becomes gold," and so forth.
Copper is indeed well-known in the world; it clearly does not attain the state of gold, that is, the nature of being gold.
"Even by great afflictions," "even from great affliction," or even by mental outbursts (*manasphutkāra*) and the like—of whom?

Of living beings. This [refers to] wisdom (*prajñā*), which according to the traditionalists consists of karma and volition (*saṅkalpa*); its "lotus" (*paṅkaja*) is the [wisdom-]lotus; its "service" (*sevā*) is the attainment (*samāpatti*) together with it. Even by that, "innate bliss" (*sahajānanda*), characterized by unobscured great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is not "conceived" (*sambhāvyate*), meaning it is not directly realized.
Since this is so, therefore those for whom— in addition to the previously explained cultivation of wisdom— there are innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) and the rest,
who possess bodies that are accumulations of merit and who bear forms composed of merit,
are "local" (*prādeśika*), meaning they abide in specific regions.
In some place, in a certain region, they are born together with [the consort].

*Mudrā* is wisdom (*prajñā*), which has already been explained; by means of her, there is the *kunduru*, characterized by the union of the two organs. Therein, for one whose mind is waveless—whose consciousness is free from all conceptual constructions—the *siddhas* are those who have attained *mahāmudrā*; furthermore, they do not possess the same nature as other ordinary beings.
To them we offer our salutation by bowing down with all our limbs. By this, the following is illuminated:

for all those who do not know the oral tradition (*apasampradāya*) and whose roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) have not been accumulated, there is no attainment of Mahāmudrā in any way due to the absence of the aforementioned application of wisdom (*prajñāyoga*).
However, for those who know the tradition and have accumulated roots of merit, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā occurs even through the application of wisdom previously explained. || 1 ||
That consciousness which was described by the Blessed One through the union of the vajra and the lotus—where is it for sentient beings who have not received the oral transmission?

For them, supreme detachment from passion arises from the instruction on innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) situated between the two joys; furthermore, their state of non-emission (*akṣaratā*) is established through bliss as the firm conviction in the *mudrā*. II.2.

Now, he clarifies through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) the very same meaning established in the preceding verse, beginning with "That consciousness" (*yā saṃvit*). That consciousness,
characterized by unobscured great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which has been described and established in every respect as being born from the *Yoginītantra*, *Yogatant*ra, and so forth—
By the Blessed One, through the union of the vajra and the lotus—by virtue of his nature as the inseparable unity of the four bodies of unobstructed great bliss—as previously described;
the sense is that for whom would she not exist?

[She exists] for those beings who are ignorant of the oral tradition, whose roots of merit are not yet accumulated, and whose heads have not been immersed in the rows of dust from the feet of the glorious Guru.
In the case of departing from the lineage transmission, there is a departure from the path.
Following upon the characteristics of passion—namely, *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, and *sahajānanda*—there subsequently arises dispassion (*virāga*), characterized by the moment of emission.
However, the arising of unobstructed great bliss does not occur during the state of *sahajānanda*.
However, those who know the tradition [explain it as follows]: "The innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) which resides between the two joys" refers to that innate gnosis situated between the two joys.

From the instruction regarding that—by means of which instruction all conceptual constructions are understood right there—the unobscured arising of great bliss occurs, characterized by the non-emission of the *bodhicitta*.

Furthermore, in every respect, for those masters of yoga, the state of the immutable (*akṣaratā*) is established through bliss; it is realized through the bliss of the immutable by virtue of the non-emission of the *bodhicitta*.

Regarding the "abiding in the conviction of the *mudrā*": the *mudrā* is the *mahāmudrā*; "conviction" (*adhimukti*) is its realization; and those who abide—that is, remain—by means of that [realization] in a state consisting of constant bliss are indeed the accomplished ones of *mahāmudrā* (*mahāmudrāsiddha*). This is to be connected with the preceding verse. (2)

Therein, at first, having abandoned the pleasure of woman at the intermediate moment of the "cessation" (virama)—which is the state of passion for all remaining stages—one who, absorbed in that, grasps the other, the immutable bliss (akṣarasukha), is the illustrious one; wise and skilled in the procedure of sealing with camphor by the command of the Guru, his mind reeling from drinking the wine of self-bliss, he does not fall into delusion. || 3 ||
Now, the knower of the tradition speaks of the excellence of its power: "In that regard, at the beginning," and so forth.

In that regard, within that innate characteristic (*sahaja-lakṣaṇa*), having first abandoned the female pleasure—which belongs to the intermediate moment between passion and dispassion, at the final stage of the "remainder" (*śeṣapada*) characterized by the moment of emission (*cyuti*) following the "cessation" (*virama*) of the blisses of joy, supreme joy, and cessation—one grasps and realizes another, imperishable (*akṣara*) bliss. This bliss, whose characteristic is as previously described, is attained through the embrace of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, rather than from the melting bliss previously obtained through the meditative absorption of the two mudrās.

Moreover, he who is absorbed in that becomes one with it; by removing all conceptual constructions, he remains as a form consisting of perpetual bliss. He is the illustrious one, whose form is constantly embraced by emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
He alone is skilled in the procedure of sealing with camphor regarding the non-falling of the *bodhicitta*.
How so?

By the command of the Guru, characterized by both speech and silence, he states the result: "For his mind is reeling from drinking the nectar of his own bliss. This "bliss" (ānanda) is innate bliss (sahajānanda), characterized by unobscured great happiness (mahāsukha).
That very [bliss] is the nectar (āsava), the wine.

His drinking is the intense savoring; by that, his mind is reeling, meaning his mind has departed from all conceptual constructions. The wise one does not approach—that is, he does not attain again—the delusion characterized by the moment of death, because his intellect is unobstructed due to the departure of all conceptual constructions. || 3 ||
What talk can there be here on this path between those whose intellects are refined by the proper method of moving through herds of cows and Meru, the abode of the thunderbolt?
For from this very foundation, for the wise man who has attained impetuosity at the feet of the Guru, the union with wisdom itself becomes the unsurpassed state.
Now, with reference to those beings who are vessels and non-vessels for right knowledge, he says: "Like the manner of a herd of cows," and so forth.

Just as there is a sequential movement for a herd—a collection—of cows, so too, by whatever path one cow goes, other cows also go by that very same path; in that case, there is no deliberation regarding whether it is a good path or a bad path. Likewise, what talk can there be of those whose intellects are merely conventional, who act without reflection, and whose nature is equal to that of beasts? Their... [is as follows].
Of such [beings]:
here on this path, for those like Meru who are struck by the thunderbolt, the vajra-pada alone is the Sumeru, because it is not understood by ordinary people.
On that same path here—characterized by the Mahāyāna which follows the sequence of mantras—it is to be maintained by those whose minds are exceedingly fickle.

But for those great ones who have correctly accumulated their own roots of virtue, whose feet-dust of the true guru has been worshipped through a succession of many lifetimes—for them, by virtue of this empowerment which is about to be explained, characterized by the wisdom of self-empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and arising from the fervor born at the feet of the guru; with all conceptual constructions dissolved within the very particles of the dust of the glorious guru’s feet, and out of joy;
through the embrace of emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects by oneself alone in the union of wisdom (*prajñā-saṅga*).
It comes to be; it is accomplished.
For the skillful one who has fully accumulated the roots of merit, there arises the unsurpassed state, the state of the Great Vajradhara, which surpasses all others. || 4 ||
The Guru draws the mind away from its own substrate and instantly produces for the wise that self-realized knowledge which is otherwise difficult to attain;
for the sun-gem blazes forth suddenly when in contact with a wick. Such is the nature of things in the three worlds—it cannot be constrained by any means whatsoever.
"From the Guru," and so forth.

The Guru is the venerable teacher who knows the knowledge of self-mastery (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). From self-mastery—that is, from the excellence of the power of self-mastery—he withdraws the mind of the wise.

As the mind undergoes transformation through the state of being both with and without thought, the mind of the disciple—provided he is truly a disciple among the wise—attains a self-cognized knowledge that is not merely this much;
rather, it instantaneously produces a knowledge unperceivable by others within the disciple’s continuum.
The meaning is that this occurs at the very moment he is empowered, and not after some interval of time.
Meditation itself is the state of being.
Even that which is difficult to obtain— unattainable even over a succession of many lifetimes by those who have not accumulated roots of merit—
is clarified by means of this very illustration.

"In whatever way it may be, it has cotton as its limiting adjunct" (*milattūlopādhi*): that of which the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the very cotton (*tūla*) which is meeting (*milat*)—that is, becoming proximate—is the cause;
it burns, that is, it becomes possessed of fire (*sāgni*).
At that very moment, the sun-gem—the *sūryakānta*—[spontaneously] acts;

for the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things, which consists in their excellence at producing effects, can somehow be applied [to explain phenomena], but how could it ever be subject to further questioning within the three worlds, including the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the rest? || 5 ||
Whatever has been understood by those who know themselves on the various paths that are somewhat subject to division, O wise ones, contains no fault whatsoever here.
Therefore, through the application of wisdom, superior resolution arises; and beyond the guru’s own self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), there is no third object.

Whatever has been attained and directly realized by us, the followers of the Daudīpāda tradition—something within the scope of all conceptualization yet self-cognized, characterized as unobstructed great bliss (*anāvaraṇa-mahāsukha*) along the various paths of the Mantra and Mahāyāna systems—that has been spoken and written by our own wise ones according to their respective insights.
O scholars, there is no fault whatsoever here; there is no fault at all on this path.
Therefore, from the previously explained application of wisdom (*prajñā-yoga*), there arises— that is, it is excellently accomplished—
concentration (*samādhāna*), which is the setting of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and is superior, possessing excellence. It is not merely this much.
This supreme [state] is accomplished through these two alone—the Guru’s own abode (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) as already mentioned and as yet to be described.
Furthermore, there is no third object; one should not entertain in one's own mind the notion that there exists such a third source for the arising of knowledge apart from these two.

This has been stated primarily because [the author] will later describe the arising of knowledge in some individuals even from the tasting of wine (*madanāsvāda*), such as *goṅkā* and so forth. This indeed is the *Yogīśvaracūḍāmaṇi*. (6)

At the end of passion, at the moment of entering the state of cessation, when the moon is established in its own nature, that consciousness which is the activity of the mind, or the other [state] in which the flow of the breath is obstructed—at that time, that supreme state which is bliss arising from no other source is directly realized; he who possesses such self-experience therein is indeed perfected through Mahāmudrā.

At the end of passion—specifically at the moment of *sahaja* following the sequence of *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, and *viramānanda*, at the time of entering *virama* when the moment of emission is imminent—in that *sahaja* state, which abides as the nature of *bodhicitta* within the moon, and which has been transformed into the nature of unobscured great bliss through the cessation of all conceptual constructions, there arises a further activity of the mind characterized by non-conceptual, true bliss; this supreme activity is wisdom (*dhī*). (XLVI) Because all conceptual constructions have subsided, it consists of perpetual bliss;
the flow of the vital wind is arrested.
In every respect, there is the non-conducting of the wind even within the six middle cakras due to the cessation of the [ordinary] course.

At that time, during the stage of the limb of meditative absorption immediately following *anusmṛti*, there is a bliss that cannot arise from anything else; it is the state of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), perceivable by the masters of yoga through non-conceptualization. That very state is the supreme reality (*param padam*) itself; it is the direct state of omniscience. For whichever yogin has his own experience in that place—in that state—his direct realization of Mahāvajradhara is such that he is a perfected one (*siddha*) through Mahāmudrā; he is indeed accomplished by Mahāmudrā, of this there is no doubt. (7)
Without the application of wisdom, he instantly brings about the state of the Vajra for the virtuous; or rather, through that very application, by acting as an awakener like the cool-rayed moon.
He who knows the empowerment is the Guru here, and no other; such is his power that it strikes the mind instantly, like a wicked man. (8)

Without the previously mentioned application of wisdom, the glorious Guru instantly effects [the attainment of] the state of Vajra, which is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, immediately following the empowerment,
for those virtuous ones who have accumulated unsurpassed roots of merit.
Or rather, because of that yoga, it causes the awakening of the cool-rayed moon for those who already exist [as vessels], by obstructing the outward movement of the *bodhicitta*.
For this reason, he is "one who knows the empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhānajña*),
meaning one in whose mind the knowledge of self-empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhānajñāna*) resides.
In this Vajrayāna, he alone is the supreme guru; no other person is so,
because others lack such extraordinary knowledge and power.

Its "power" is its extraordinary capacity, by which it strikes the mind—that is, the consciousness—residing within the continuum of the disciple, instantly and suddenly transforming it into non-mind (*acittatā*).
Even a wicked person suddenly deprives a living being of life;
this [power] is similar because it likewise deprives the mind, characterized as life, of its existence. (8)

The moment arising between the two joys is so extremely subtle that it is not perceived; how, then, can one at that time bring about the state through the union of the vajra and the lotus with the mind?
Therefore, the virtuous diligently resort to the bliss of the immutable alone; having remained there for a long time in meditative absorption, the person attains the reality once again. || 1 ||
The moment arising between the two joys has indeed been explained as the innate (*sahaja*).
That moment is extremely subtle because it lasts for only a very brief duration;
it is not perceived nor correctly ascertained by those who know the oral tradition.
At that time, when [the drops] are extremely subtle,
how does one act with the mind, and how does one comprehend with the consciousness?
Through the union of the vajra and lotus, by means of the meditative absorption of the two organs.

The "place" (*pada*) is the state of Mahāmudrā; therefore, through the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), the very bliss of the immutable (*akṣarasaukhya*) arises as the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *bodhicitta*. This is that which is diligently resorted to with great excellence by noble beings, the lords of yogins.

Having stood, that is, having become established; there, in the state of outflow (*niṣyanda*), for a long time and for a long duration, a person who is concentrated— that is, one who has attained meditative absorption—
grasps, meaning he realizes it.
Furthermore, the meaning is that reality (tattva) becomes the fourth. || 9 ||
Is the water of the mirage to be grasped, like the throbbing of a tortoise’s eye, for those who exert themselves in yoga through the pure waters of direct consciousness?
That state of experience arises only from long-term persistence; once the moon has set, there is indeed nothing further to be done here by means of a thunderbolt.
He states that [the mind] is perfectly co-emergent with the following words: "Why water in a mirage? and so forth.
Why would water in a mirage be graspable? Because it is entirely non-existent there.
It is only through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) that there is the appearance of water therein.

Where [is] the direct cognition (*sākṣāt-saṃvit*)—the knowledge of unobscured great bliss—at the moment of the innate instant of the external two-fold sense-faculties? It is like the opening and closing of the eyes of a *kamaṭha*; *kamaṭha* is a specific type of aquatic creature, referring here to its extremely rapid blinking of the eyes, though by the word *kamaṭha* a tortoise is not meant. At that moment, there is no direct perception. It is the knowledge of unobscured great bliss.
For those who possess the fatigue of the yoga involving the movement of vital energy (*prāṇa*) and who experience mere exhaustion through the union of the two external sense organs,

there arises the state of unobstructed great bliss (*anāvaraṇa-mahāsukha*), due to the long-term abiding in the innate state (*sahaja-daśā*) and the outflow of the *bodhicitta*. This occurs through the embrace of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
When the moon has departed and the *bodhicitta* has dissolved, there is indeed no further task whatsoever here.
This does not refer to external meditative attainments; for "here" means that the goal is characterized by great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
There is not even the slightest opportunity for anything else.

Likewise, it is said in the *Kālacakra*: "Sin arises from the destruction of passion, and from that, hatred is born; the one whose nature is hatred is destroyed by the falling of his own vajra, and the mind remains perpetually in a state of stupor.
In this regard, all engagement with excellent food, drink, and so forth deludes the mind; its happiness destroyed, it wanders through six births. (10)

If that absolute bliss which was previously attained through union with a beloved were indeed [the goal] now, what further excellence would there be in attaining the Seal (mudrā)? Here, there exists another [bliss] distinct from the objects of worldly pleasure external to consciousness; therefore, this other, certain Sahaja-Sukha-Śambhu manifests. || 11 ||
Now he describes the superiority of unobstructed great bliss over the bliss of the external union of the two sense organs, beginning with "from the embrace of the beloved" and so forth.
"From the embrace of the beloved" refers to that characterized by the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) of karma;
"previously" means during the state of their sexual enjoyment.
If that which has been attained and experienced—

the ultimate bliss in comparison to other worldly pleasures— is indeed external bliss, then why, even at the stage of the support (*adhiṣṭhāna*), should one abandon the experience of external mudrā-bliss? Why, for what reason?
The attainment of the *varamudrā* is the pursuit of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects for the lords of yogins. Here,

within this emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, that which is established as real— whether it be consciousness (*saṃvit*) or perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)— arises as something superior to great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
There exists something else, other than the objects of external pleasure;
it is superior to that—
that is, superior to that external pleasure.
This is some other Sahaja-Sukha-Śambhu who prevails;
characterized by self-arisen gnosis (svayambhū-jñāna) of unobscured great bliss, he proceeds with excellence. || 11 ||

Through the Guru’s own abiding state (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), the dissolution of the senses occurs for the wise; from that dissolution, pure consciousness alone radiates independently throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, nothing else whatsoever is known as a further or superior reality—those who have asserted otherwise possess bodies whose lower [teachings] are shattered by contradiction. (12)

Now, he explains how, through the power of the knowledge of the glorious Guru’s own empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), a special excellence arises within the lineage of a true disciple— beginning with the words "of the Guru" and so forth;
that is, from the Guru’s own empowerment,
which is the power of the glorious Guru’s knowledge of his own empowerment.
For the wise who have accumulated roots of virtue and follow through wisdom and faith,
there first occurs the dissolution of the faculties (*indriya-laya*), which is the entry of the faculties into luminosity; from this arisen dissolution of the faculties...
Pure consciousness alone— mere non-conceptual knowledge— manifests clearly and independently throughout the three worlds,
due to the subsiding of all mental constructions.

In the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, or in body, speech, and mind, there is nothing else whatsoever— whether it be another reality (*tattva*), something superior (*adhika*) or more excellent (*sātiśaya*), or something further (*apara*)— that has been established, realized, directly perceived, affirmed, or stabilized by those preeminent persons other than the Perfect Knowledge already set forth; they possess bodies that accord with the "breaker of the lower" (*bhiduradhara*), where "the breaker of the lower" (*bhiduradhara*) refers to the Great Vajradhara.
Those whose bodies correspond with him, possessing limbs equal in form to those of the Great Vajradhara,
are indeed Great Vajradharas themselves— such extraordinary holy beings.
The sense is that nothing else should be introduced into the mind. || 12 ||
Even though he was born in a blessed abode and performed excellent deeds as a god, this is some inexplicable power that resonates within him;
for, due to the absence of such power, a man who is a lord of yoga is like a beast, and even a god is empty within, his body fashioned from hard and heavy stone.

Now, regarding the knowledge of the empowerment of the support (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñānādhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*), he states the positive and negative concomitance (*dṛṣṭānvayavyatireka*) beginning with "in the support" (*adhiṣṭhāne*) and so forth:
when the support has arisen— that is, when the blessed knowledge of one's own empowerment has been attained by the Lord of Yogins who has acquired excellence.
Likewise, even in a god who has performed excellent deeds, and even in a god such as Śakra who has attained praiseworthy karma, there is a certain, ineffable majesty— an excellence of power—
which makes that [reality] resound, that is, it establishes it as something to be pointed out by the demonstrative "this."

If that [power] is not deposited within and established in the mind, then due to the absence—meaning the non-existence—of the majesty produced by the venerable Guru, one is like a beast; because of the lack of majesty, one is equal to beasts.
Just as a man who is a master of yoga (yogeśvara), so too is a god (sura) empty within; even a deity is empty within, devoid of majesty, his body fashioned from stone that is neither soft nor heavy.
His body was fashioned from stone characterized by soft, large, and hard fragments; his form was identical to that [of the other]. || 13 ||

Due to the absence of practice, from this lack of realization of the path, from the absence of verbal instruction, spontaneously and effortlessly, constantly and directly, and immediately through the bliss of the Guru’s command, when the entire multitude of the senses has ceased, that which arises as mere self-awareness is called the "substratum" (adhiṣṭhāna). ||14||

He states the thorough knowledge of the nature of the wisdom of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānajñāna*) with the words beginning "due to lack of practice" (*anabhyāsāt*): due to lack of practice— that is, due to the lack of practice in hearing, reflection, and meditation— from this which has been personally realized.
Precisely because of the non-attainment of the path previously explained— that is, due to the failure to attain the path of right knowledge—
and precisely because of the non-speaking, that is, the failure to speak, of right knowledge, [this occurs] suddenly, immediately following the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by the illustrious Guru.
Without affliction, constantly, uninterruptedly, directly, through immediate perception itself, and instantly— that is, at that very moment.
Due to the bliss of the Guru’s command— that is, due to the extraordinary power of the mind’s bliss arising from the venerable Guru—
and because the entire collection of sense organs has ceased to function (this being an indicative term for the cessation of all perceptions of the elements and so forth as well).

That which arises— which is mere self-awareness resulting from the departure of conceptualization and is nothing but non-conceptual awareness— is designated by the term *svādhiṣṭhāna* (self-mastery), as it is called the "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). || 14 ||

In this world, he who—having assumed a body of a Lord of Yogins produced through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)—does not cast off the mire of his senses, which resembles the sloughed skin of a snake;
he, being a connoisseur of incessant mental fluctuations seized by passion and the like, does not enter the Goddess of Consciousness, just as oil does not penetrate into water. (15)
Now, he explains the arising or non-arising of the fruit based on the arising or non-arising of the knowledge of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), beginning with the words "here" and so forth.

Here, in the sequence of self-consecration, one possesses a body of a Lord of Yogins (*yogeśvara*) produced by the sequence of self-consecration—that is, one whose body of a Lord of Yogins has been generated and accomplished through the sequence of self-consecration; this is the body of the Great Vajradhara. This [mention of the body] is an elliptical expression for the sense faculties (*akṣa*).
It abandons and completely relinquishes the mud characterized by the afflictive and cognitive obscurations of all the elements, aggregates, and so forth;
the meaning is that it is similar to the sloughing off of a snake's skin.
Just as a serpent sheds its slough, so does the Lord of Yogis [shed] the veil of afflictions and the veil of the knowable.

One who is grasped by entities, overcome by passion and the like—whose mental activity is incessantly driven by attachment, aversion, and delusion, and who is addicted to the constant flickering of the mind—does not enter the Goddess of Consciousness, the Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects; his mind does not become immersed therein.
Just as water does not enter oil in any way, so too he whose mind is excessively fickle does not enter the Goddess of Consciousness; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 15 ||
Those who relish these five vices go to the dark well of sin; if not, they go to liberation, having abandoned the distinctions of the heavenly realms.
How then can you enter into doubt through the pride of non-dualism? Who else indeed sports upon the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra?
Now, he states the distinction for those who have not yet generated the noble path and who enjoy the five sensual pleasures merely through non-conceptual pride: "This," and so forth.
This very thing, characterized by the five sensual pleasures, is itself a calamity because it results in being cast into hell.

In this [state], those who are connoisseurs (*rasika*) with longing glances go—that is, they proceed—to the dark well of sin (*pāpāndhakūpa*), a specific hell named the Dark Well brought about by the presence of sinful causes; provided that they do not possess the nature of returning there [to cyclic existence]. If they are such that they have turned away from it, then they go to liberation (*mokṣa*), characterized by various kinds of heavens; this is the connection with what precedes.

[From] the *Guhyāvalī-vivṛti*: When they have abandoned their stations—that is, when they have relinquished the locus of the five desires—by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), due to the differentiation of the earth [into realms] such as the distinction between the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and others...

Therefore, how is it that you enter into this aforementioned doubt regarding the connection with the elements (*bhūta*), and how is it that you become subject to it? This refers to [the state] arising from the pride of non-conceptuality— that is, from non-conceptual egoism— because through the direct realization of non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the enjoyment of the five objects of desire brings about security.

But he does not dwell in the ocean of saṃsāra out of conceptual construction or pride; and who, moreover, goes to the further shore of that ocean of saṃsāra? Indeed, it is someone who becomes such as this—he is truly a perfected one (siddha). To him, salutation is due in every way; this [idea] is to be connected with the very first verse.

These five lead men to the further shore of the river of delusion, like a boat; yet there is one supreme obstacle to the remover of calamities: this great, world-roaming elephant of the senses, intoxicated by the drinking of wine—charming with its attachment to the objects of the senses—which rushes toward this earth.
Now he clarifies the very same point stated in the previous verse,
saying "these five lead": these five— form, sound, smell, taste, and touch— lead, that is, bring to, the further shore of the river of delusion,
the shore of the stream of ignorance, for men, just as a boat leads one to the other shore.

In the same way, it should be connected that these [objects] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are also for the sake of another; however, there is a contradiction because the reason is fallacious (*vivartha*),
for there exists something else that is supreme (*param*) and exceedingly great due to being the cause of an excellence (*atiśaya*).

Who is he? It is the passion for the senses, characterized by attachment to the organs; that itself is like the drinking of beautiful wine, an intense tasting of liquor. By this, the mind is intoxicated—that very mind which discerns between the right and wrong path—and it is that [mind] which, throbbing with power, is unassailable.
"This is the lord of scent-elephants; that is the fragrant elephant;
this one, rushing toward this cow, is the cause of calamities."
Even association with wine and women leads a man to the state of Indra; yet, O wise one, that which is grasped here is not abandoned.
For one [of these] is the pleasure born from the bliss of experiencing the five objects of sense, while the second is the entire world, both moving and unmoving, pervading all.
He clarifies the very same point mentioned previously with the words "even association with a divine woman," and so forth.

"Divine" (*sura*) refers to intoxicating liquor; "woman" (*nārī*) refers to association with a woman who is the object of one's karmic intentions, characterized by drinking and sexual union. The word "even" (*api*) is used in a conjunctive sense.

It "brings about" (*upanayati*), meaning it causes [the practitioner] to attain, in relation to the knowledge of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*). This is an elliptical expression referring to the male practitioner.

Even for women, what is the state of the thunderbolt? It is the state of the Great Vajra-holder. When does that state of the thunderbolt belong to him? When, here in this world, union with a divine woman occurs—a worldly existence brought about by wisdom, which is a continuum of dependently originated phenomena.

"Wisdom" (*dhīmattva*) is its intrinsic nature; "established by those two" means bound to them. The meaning is that if one's mind is bound to the union (*yuganaddha*), he states the result: "That which is one"—that is, because it is one, being devoid of wisdom due to objective apprehension (*sopalambha*) among the five [objects] beginning with form.

The bliss born from the joy of the flavor of experience is merely bound to the savoring of the bliss arising from the experience of the five sense objects; the second is the bliss produced from emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, which pervades that [first], pervades the objects such as form and so forth, and extends beyond them to the entire triple world—the whole of existence, both stable and moving, stationary and living, without exception.

This very state of consciousness, born from the lineage succession of the Guru, is indeed that foundation which is celebrated through the words of oneself and others.
Just as a lamp arises from a lamp, and from that other lamps are likewise produced in succession, what cause for wonder can there be here?
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars (||) and does not contain any content to translate.]
Now, he expresses amazement at the power of the knowledge born of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), beginning with the words "by the lineage of the Guru" (*guroḥ pāramparyakramāt*).

"Of the Guru" means of the venerable Guru (*śrīguru*); "the lineage of succession" (*pāramparyakrama*) refers to the lineage of venerable Gurus (*śrīguruparamparā*). That which is produced or accomplished by that [lineage] is the state of consciousness (*saṃvitpada*), the knowledge born of self-consecration; this alone is it.
That very thing is the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*), characterized as the knowledge of self-consecration.

It is proclaimed— that is, it is loudly celebrated— by one's own words, by one's own utterances, by the words of the Blessed One such as "The vajra-penetration, the great penetration" (*vajrāveśo mahāveśaḥ*) and so forth as recited in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, and by the words of others, namely by the treatises composed by Maheśvara (*maheśapraṇīta*) which expound the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration.
Just as one lamp arises from another—that is, it comes into being preeminently—and from that very lamp other lamps are born, and further lamps are produced successively, one after another;
what is there to wonder at here? What is the cause for those of marvelous intellect—those whose minds are struck with astonishment?

In the empty abode where the blazing flames of the rising fire are constantly manifest, the fool who worships that [fire] with effort finds happiness therein;
yet the splendor of the streak of dust upon the head, produced by hundreds of prostrations at the lotus feet of the Guru, swiftly bestows the state of a Vajra-holder.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context function as a section divider. [Section Break]

Now, [the author] speaks of the mental joy arising from the knowledge of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and its cause, beginning with the words "the blossoming of blazing flames" (*jvalajjvālonmīlana*).

Blazing flames: that flame which causes [everything] to blaze is a "blazing flame. By that, it is "blossoming," meaning becoming clear. The "blossoming of blazing flames" refers to the fire of gnosis (*jñānānala*); [the bliss] is constant within that.

Day and night, in the empty abode—the dwelling of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects—he who is dull and of dull intellect, yet who diligently honors and serves that great fire of primordial wisdom with exceptional faith, becomes happy through the attainment of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
In that regard, when emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is realized within oneself, one directly perceives the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); such is the meaning.

The lotus-foot of the Guru, the illustrious Guru—the path of perfect knowledge—takes refuge; therein lies prostration by means of the eight limbs and so forth. "A hundred" is an indicative mark for a multitude of such acts.

Adorned and perfectly embellished by that [prostration], the head of the disciple—that upon which the line of dust, the trail of pollen from the lotus-foot of the True Guru, leaves its mark—immediately, at the very moment of touching the head, brings about and accomplishes the Vajra-path, the Mahāmudrā. One should by no means entertain any doubt regarding this.

Whether the Guru is near or far, what does it matter? What kind of talk is this regarding an ignorant child? The accomplishment of consciousness occurs suddenly even across hundreds of leagues.
The sun shines in the expanse of the sky, and the lotus blooms in the pond; is the power of the capable ever a cause for wonder?
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context function as a section divider or punctuation mark. [End of Section]
Now, he demonstrates the arising of perfect knowledge for good disciples even when the venerable Guru is far away or not in their presence—with the verse beginning "adūre dūre vā" and so forth.

Whether "near," meaning in the presence of the true Guru, or "far," meaning even a hundred *yojanas* away from the true Guru; here, on the path of the knowledge of one’s own *svādhiṣṭhāna*, what talk, what conversation can there be? What [talk] is "non-existent" (*asatī*), meaning it does not exist, because the accomplishment of consciousness (*saṃvitsiddhi*) occurs—comes to fruition—for the child, that is, the good disciple, suddenly and instantly, even across hundreds of *yojanas*, extending beyond the distance of a hundred *yojanas*.
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration:
the sun (bhānu) exists in the portion of the sky (nabhobhāga), that is, in the region of space (ākāśadeśa),
and yet it shines forth and attains illumination.

The lotus (*saroja*)—the *padma*—in a lake (*sarasi*), that is, in a pond, possesses power (*prabhāva*), an excellence (*atiśaya*), belonging to those who are capable (*śaktānām*), meaning those endowed with efficacy.
Is this a cause for wonder? On the contrary, this is not a cause for wonder at all.

The knowledge of reality is twofold: that which is expressible through speech and that which is inexpressible; one proceeds from the limbs [of yoga] while the other proceeds from the bodiless [inner self].

That which, when these two are unified, constantly arises through diligent application and is spontaneously accomplished, is this very Guru who is heavy with the higher path that shatters the lower way.

XLVI. Wisdom: I am that very Lord Heruka, who is not divided within me.

By performing this entire sequence—with the venerable lotus, the intoxicant, and the cow-dung fire—according to the prescribed reverence, the Lord of Yogins succeeds with a mind focused on that which is beyond the senses.
A living being is a person; in ultimate reality, every one of them has the nature of Mahāvajradhara. You, too, must understand it in exactly that way.
By this, he instructs you that there arises a supreme, inverted understanding.
Likewise, "Kapālin" refers to the consort; "Kapālī" refers to Mahāvajradhara.
He protects (pālayati) and sustains (dhatte) *ka*—the unobstructed great bliss—by way of its manifestation through the ascent to the *uṣṇīṣa*, and by way of the complete fulfillment of all limbs.
His consort is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects; he is equal to and identical with her.
The world is the infinite and boundless realm of worlds.
Its female folk are those in the form of women, while I am the yogin’s own form; indeed, the Blessed One is the very embodiment of Heruka.
One should realize: "I am indeed that which is designated by the term Heruka.

By this, it is indicated that the entire universe has the nature of the conceptualized maṇḍala-circle; you must also comprehend this: that nothing whatsoever exists as distinct from me. With a non-conceptual mind, one should understand that there is nothing at all that remains separate from me, but rather that everything is included within me.

The "glorious lotus" (*śrīpadma*) is the lotus of the woman who is the embodiment of ritual intention (*karmasaṅkalpa*), while "madana" refers to wine. Together with these, there are ten substances including cow dung and so forth;

performing and utilizing the glorious lotus and madana along with these, one should do so according to their relative importance—that is, according to which is superior and how one enjoys them—yet all of this is set forth here in the verse.
With a mind that transcends the senses and has passed beyond all mental constructions of the sense-faculties,
he becomes a lord of yoga— the crest-jewel of the masters of yoga—
and attains perfection.

In some cases through the application of wisdom (*prajñā*), in some through the nectar of the five sense-pleasures, in some through self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), and in some through the path of the Guru’s word;

according to the diversity of inclination in men, the one whose hands are marked with the vajra reveals his own accomplishment—there is nothing to be achieved for us that is not within the range of speech.

Now, by means of cultivating whichever object whatsoever, the arising of the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*), characterized by the unobstructed great bliss of those sentient beings, is accomplished.
Regarding this, it says "in some places," and so forth.
"In some places" is an indication of [specific] location and time.
In a certain place and at a certain time, for someone who has accumulated roots of merit and whose birth is characterized by extraordinary fortune,
it should be connected [to the following]: because of the application of the two types of wisdom previously explained,
he manifests his own nature as the arising of unobscured great bliss.
In some cases, it arises from the bliss of the five immortal sense-faculties and from the bliss produced by the five sense-faculties and their five objects;
in some cases, from self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), due to the extraordinary power of the spiritual friend who knows self-consecration;
and from the path of the guru’s words, characterized by the hearing of the guru’s instructions.
Not everywhere, but in some particular place;
due to the diversity of inclinations and their corresponding lineages (*gotra*),
the Great Vajradhara— whose hands are marked with vajras— manifests and makes clear his own self within a person who is a supreme being.

For this very reason, that which is self-established (*svasiddha*) for us—something attained by itself without effort, which is a state beyond the reach of speech, a state transcending the path of words—is that which is called Mahāmudrā.
Alternatively, "self-established" means that such knowledge is already established for all, because its nature is the union (*yuganaddha*);
"not to be accomplished" (*no sādhya*) means it is not something to be achieved.
Furthermore, in all cases, it is as previously described.
O wise ones, I have not heard any other tantra here, nor do I possess any knowledge regarding the discussions on categories of existence.
If this *Guhyāvalī* flashes forth due to my devotion to the dust of the lotus feet of my Guru, what can I do?

Thus ends the Guhyāvalī composed by Dauḍīpāda.
Now, *Dhīḥ* states that knowledge alone is the means for accomplishing all goals, beginning with the words "another tantra" (*tantrāntaram*) and so forth.

"Another tantra" refers to the *Yoginītantra* and others; what need is there to mention merely hearing them? As for the contemplation and meditation upon them, it is even further removed. In this regard, regarding the performance of the *Guhyāvalī*, I possess no knowledge at all—not even the slightest bit of knowledge exists within me.
There is no correct knowledge for me, nor do I possess it.

Furthermore, among discourses on categories (*padārtha*), there is for me no discourse—that is, no discussion—concerning the meaning of nouns ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) or verbs ending in tense-suffixes (*tiṅanta*).
O wise ones, those whose intellects are completely purified!
Through devotion to the lotus feet of the Guru and through affection for the dust of the Guru’s lotus feet,
the *Guhyāvalī*— the series of secret causes for the arising of the knowledge of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*— which is the collection of texts explaining that [knowledge],
may it itself manifest and become clearly evident.
"What then shall I do? I have no power in this matter;
rather, the mere touch of the dust from the lotus feet of a true guru is my only refuge"—this is the intended meaning. || 25 ||
By whatever merit I have gained from this commentary on the *Guhyāvalī*, may there indeed be the glory of enlightenment for the entire world;
and by virtue of all the unwholesome karma produced by all sentient beings, may I become like a swan amidst lotuses, even while surrounded by the fires of hell.
The Commentary on the Guhyāvalī.
Commentary: by the learned elder Śrīghanadeva.
